articles.title: ‘Money alone won’t get us there’: UN steps up aid for 12 forgotten crises
articles.summary: Getting aid to people in the world’s most neglected emergencies takes more than money. It takes open roads, open borders and leaders willing to help it reach those in dire need.
articles.content:
That was the message from UN relief chief Tom Fletcher on Friday, as the aid coordination office he runs, OCHA, released $160 million to keep life-saving help flowing in 12 of the most underfunded crises on the planet.

“We have 87 million people to reach, and no time to waste,” said Mr. Fletcher, the Emergency Relief Coordinator.

Tweet URL

“Today’s new funding will help us get aid to people who might otherwise be left behind. But money alone won’t get us there: leaders must exercise political will to open access, remove obstacles and help us reach people whose lives are on the line.”

The 87 million are the world’s needy facing the most severe crises this year.

Access the sticking point

Five of the 12 crises – Afghanistan, the Occupied Palestinian Territory, South Sudan, Sudan and Yemen – are among 10 contexts where Mr. Fletcher has called for urgent diplomatic action to secure access. Unlocking it would open the way to assistance for 11 million people.

The bulk of the allocation, $150 million, comes from the UN’s Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) and will be shared out as follows:

Afghanistan, the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Yemen : $18 million each

: $18 million each Somalia and Sudan : $16 million each

: $16 million each South Sudan : $15 million

: $15 million Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger : $10 million each

: $10 million each Chad : $9 million

: $9 million Cameroon : $6 million

: $6 million Cuba: $4 million

Including people with disabilities

A further $10 million is set aside for people with disabilities in the same 12 crises, so that aid reaches them and works for them.

CERF is teaming up with the UN Global Disability Fund, which will add up to $4 million in funding and technical support through its Inclusion Catalyst Hub.

Part of that will go towards strengthening local organizations of people with disabilities and their role in the response.

Fast-moving fund

CERF, managed by OCHA, is one of the fastest funding tools available. Allocations for underfunded emergencies rest on analysis of more than 100 humanitarian indicators and wide consultation with partners.

Friday’s release takes CERF allocations in 2026 to $483 million.

Since the General Assembly created it in 2005, the fund has channelled some $10.2 billion to hundreds of millions of people in more than 117 countries and territories, thanks to 135 Member States and observers, along with private donors and individuals. Its annual funding target is $1 billion.

articles.title: Collective action needed to tackle global information crisis, UN-led dialogue hears
articles.summary: Governments, UN entities, civil society, media, academia and the private sector have called for stronger cooperation and practical action to respond to a rapidly changing global information landscape.
articles.content:
The call came at the high-level Information Integrity Solutions Dialogue at UN Headquarters in New York during the high-level week of the 81st session of the General Assembly.

Co-hosted by Brazil, the UN Secretariat, the UN development Programme (UNDP) and the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the event brought together practitioners and policymakers from across regions and sectors to examine how the UN Global Principles for Information Integrity and the Global Digital Compact can be put into practice.

Information integrity means ensuring reliable and accurate information is available to all, allowing people to make informed decisions, participate meaningfully in public life, and exercise their right to freedom of expression.

Participants warned that the rapid transformation of the information ecosystem, including the growing use of unregulated and untested artificial intelligence systems and other emerging technologies, is deepening existing risks.

“Today, a handful of companies still dominate and shape our global information architecture,” said Melissa Fleming, UN Under-Secretary-General for Global Communications.

“Their priorities remain the same: engagement, profit. Always placed above the public interest,” she said. “Today, information defenders – civil society, journalists, scientists and others – are still underfunded and under attack.”

“In short, we are deep into a global information crisis. The crisis has grown but so has our resolve.”

Tweet URL

From principles to practical solutions

The Dialogue also showcased how governments, organizations and communities are responding, with an emphasis on turning shared principles into solutions at national and regional levels.

Climate information integrity was a central focus. Participants highlighted the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change as a model for connecting global norms with national realities and placing the Global South at the centre of solutions.

Projects supported by the Initiative include efforts to improve public access to evidence-based research, strengthen information literacy and community communications, and advance platform accountability.

Participants said many of these approaches could also be applied to other priorities, including elections, peace and security, child online safety, the protection of human rights defenders and disaster response.

The private sector also came under scrutiny, including business models that can incentivize harmful practices online. Speakers highlighted work with advertisers to promote human-rights-responsible advertising and reduce the inadvertent funding of harmful content and practices.

Trust was another recurring theme, with participants highlighting the growing difficulty of determining what is real and identifying accurate, reliable information. Proposed solutions emphasized community outreach and direct human engagement.

“The solutions we have are as wide-ranging as the threats we face,” Ms. Fleming said. “From climate to health, to democratic governance. From prevention to response. Together, we’re pursuing those solutions.”

Building stronger networks

Participants reaffirmed information integrity and the UN Global Principles as a common framework for bringing diverse actors together in support of a safer, more humane information ecosystem.

They also called for greater exchanges of knowledge and experience across regions and sectors, as well as increased investment to sustain and expand solutions that are already working.

As a concrete next step, the UN is developing the Global Information Integrity Exchange (GIIEx), which will connect practitioners, researchers, policymakers and other stakeholders working on solutions to information threats.

It will facilitate the sharing of research, tools, training materials, and policy developments, while connecting people working towards common information-integrity goals. The UN Centres of Excellence for Information Integrity and related initiatives will feed into the Exchange.

Participants also called for a pan-African UN-African Union conference on information integrity, greater availability of research tools and stronger protections for information integrity defenders.

AI in the spotlight at UNGA81

The Dialogue was held during the Assembly’s high-level week in which artificial intelligence featured prominently in discussions on multilateralism, human rights, development, and global governance.

Opening the annual General Debate on 22 September, Secretary-General António Guterres highlighted the speed of AI development and called for reliable guardrails to limit potential harm while allowing innovation to continue. He also stressed the need to involve governments, businesses, scientists, civil society, and academia.

The impact of AI on children was also in focus. On 22 September, the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence brought together global leaders to strengthen cooperation on protecting children’s rights and safety in the digital age.

That meeting launched a roadmap covering safety by design, protection of children’s data, action against AI-enabled sexual abuse material, age assurance, AI literacy and stronger evidence on how children use AI.

Against this backdrop, the Information Integrity Solutions Dialogue examined AI as part of the wider information ecosystem and how technological change is affecting trust, access to reliable information and people’s ability to participate meaningfully in public life.

Participants closed with a call for greater collaboration across sectors and regions, so that the principles underpinning information integrity can translate into measurable action ahead of COP31, the next edition of the UN climate conference, as well as the Internet Governance Forum and beyond.

Find the Chair's Summary of the event here.

articles.title: How to respond to hate speech without fuelling it further
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 02 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03058-3Psychologist Mirta Galesic discusses an increase in hateful comments online, and the science-backed way to react.
articles.content:
The Spanish Observatory on Racism and Xenophobia reported a spike in hate posts on social media coinciding with the arrival of thousands of migrants from Morocco to the Autonomous City of Ceuta.Credit: Abu Adem Muhammed/Anadolu/Getty

Is society losing the fight against hate speech?

Hate speech — discourse that attacks a person or group on the basis of their inherent characteristics or identity — is on the rise worldwide. It can be triggered by various events, from elections and migrant crises to this year’s men’s football World Cup. Posts that were hostile to people of South Asian origin in the United States rose by 240% on the social-media platform X between January 2024 and June this year.

Hateful discourse can widen social divisions, instill ‘us versus them’ narratives and increase political polarization. Divisive rhetoric is also being exacerbated by content generated by artificial-intelligence models and bot accounts.

Scientists are keen to understand these phenomena so that they can find the most effective ways to counter them. Mirta Galesic, a co-leader of the research group Collective Minds at the Complexity Science Hub in Vienna, studies hate speech and anti-hate speech, called counterspeech. Galesic talks to Nature about strategies to tackle hateful discourse online.

Why is it an important time to study hate speech?

In some countries, polarization is quite prominent — especially ‘affective polarization’, when individuals dislike people who have different political opinions to their own. Rising inequality, shifts in power, armed conflicts and institutions not working as well as they were before create uncertainty. The accumulation of this uncertainty is easily channelled into hate towards particular groups of people.

Psychologist Mirta Galesic co-leads the Collective Minds research group in Vienna, which studies how groups of people change their beliefs, make decisions and organize themselves.Credit: Anja Boeck

And given how easy it is to lead people into thinking the worst about others — especially now, by using AI tools to create fake photos and videos — I would say that it’s extremely important to study hate speech. Everyone should be able to recognize their own susceptibility to be manipulated.

How do you research hate speech?

My colleagues and I analysed more than one million posts made between January 2015 and December 2018 on the social-media site Twitter (now known as X). These posts were responses to roughly 130,000 posts by German news organizations, journalists, bloggers and politicians. This time period started with what is sometimes referred to as the ‘migrant crisis’ in Germany, when more than one million refugees and asylum seekers moved there after a policy change allowed them to apply to stay in the nation from Germany, rather than from the first European Union country they arrived in.

In subsequent studies, we used large language models to measure hate in conversations. We also categorized numerous ways in which posters responded to each other and identified which strategies were most effective at countering hate.

What did you find were the best ways to counter hate?

If you see hate speech online, take it almost as your duty to disagree. You just say ‘I disagree’. Don’t feel pressured to have an elaborate argument. Just express your dissent — not to change the mind of the commenter, but to show people that others have a different opinion.

Next, ask friends to join and say that they also disagree.

Lastly, if you encounter a person who has an opinion that is different to yours, don’t cut them off. Try to learn more about them and find out what you share with them. You will be able to get through to them more easily after that.

Often, people are in situations in which it’s easy to encounter extreme examples online, and feelings of unease and fear can be amplified in online spaces. Humans are very social beings. We align ourselves to our environment. The more something is discussed, the more extreme people’s opinions tend to become. That’s why just showing up and saying ‘I disagree’ is so important.
articles.reasoning: The article discusses research-backed strategies to counter hate speech, a significant social issue affecting many communities worldwide. It highlights scientific efforts to understand and mitigate hateful discourse, promoting social cohesion and reducing polarization. The focus on practical, evidence-based counterspeech methods offers hope for improving online interactions and societal harmony.
articles.personality_title: Simple ways to respond to hate speech online, backed by science
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Hate speech means saying things that attack people because of who they are. It has been increasing on social media, especially during events like migrant arrivals or big sports competitions. This kind of speech can divide people and make conflicts worse.

**What happened** – Psychologist Mirta Galesic and her team studied over a million social media posts from 2015 to 2018, focusing on reactions to news about migrants in Germany. They used advanced computer tools to understand hate speech and how people respond to it. Their research found clear ways to respond to hate speech that can help reduce its spread.

**Impact** – The study shows that simply saying “I disagree” to hateful comments, even without long arguments, helps others see that hate is not the only opinion. When friends join in to disagree too, it makes a bigger difference. Also, trying to understand people with different views can open paths to better conversations. These simple steps make online spaces less hostile and help people connect rather than divide.

**What's next step** – Researchers hope this knowledge will encourage more people to speak out against hate speech online. They also want to study how these strategies work in different countries and social groups. This could lead to new tools or campaigns that support peaceful online discussions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Saying “I disagree” to hate speech online, inviting others to join, and understanding different views are effective ways to reduce hate and build better conversations.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des façons simples de répondre aux discours de haine en ligne, soutenues par la science
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les discours de haine sont des propos qui attaquent une personne ou un groupe à cause de leur identité. Ils augmentent sur les réseaux sociaux, surtout lors d’événements comme l’arrivée de migrants ou des compétitions sportives majeures. Ces discours divisent les gens et aggravent les conflits.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La psychologue Mirta Galesic et son équipe ont étudié plus d’un million de publications sur les réseaux sociaux entre 2015 et 2018, en se concentrant sur les réactions aux informations sur les migrants en Allemagne. Ils ont utilisé des outils informatiques avancés pour comprendre les discours de haine et la façon dont les gens y répondent. Leur recherche a révélé des moyens simples et efficaces de répondre à la haine.

**Impact** – L’étude montre que dire simplement « Je ne suis pas d’accord » aux commentaires haineux, même sans longs arguments, aide les autres à voir que la haine n’est pas la seule opinion. Quand des amis rejoignent pour exprimer leur désaccord, cela a un plus grand effet. Aussi, essayer de comprendre les personnes qui ont des opinions différentes peut ouvrir la voie à de meilleures conversations. Ces étapes simples rendent les espaces en ligne moins hostiles et favorisent la connexion entre les gens.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs espèrent que ces connaissances encourageront plus de personnes à s’exprimer contre les discours de haine en ligne. Ils veulent aussi étudier comment ces stratégies fonctionnent dans différents pays et groupes sociaux. Cela pourrait mener à de nouveaux outils ou campagnes pour soutenir des discussions pacifiques en ligne.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Dire « Je ne suis pas d’accord » face à la haine en ligne, inviter d’autres à faire de même, et comprendre les points de vue différents sont des moyens efficaces pour réduire la haine et améliorer les échanges.
articles.personality_title_es: Formas sencillas y científicas para responder al discurso de odio en línea

**Impacto** – El estudio muestra que decir simplemente “No estoy de acuerdo” a comentarios de odio, incluso sin argumentos largos, ayuda a que otros vean que hay opiniones diferentes. Cuando amigos se unen para decir lo mismo, el efecto es mayor. Además, tratar de entender a quienes piensan distinto puede abrir mejores conversaciones. Estos pasos simples hacen que los espacios en línea sean menos hostiles y ayudan a conectar a las personas.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan que esta información anime a más personas a hablar contra el discurso de odio en línea. También quieren estudiar cómo funcionan estas estrategias en diferentes países y grupos sociales. Esto podría crear nuevas herramientas o campañas para apoyar discusiones pacíficas en internet.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Decir “No estoy de acuerdo” al discurso de odio en línea, invitar a otros a hacer lo mismo y entender diferentes puntos de vista son maneras efectivas de reducir el odio y mejorar las conversaciones.

articles.title: Women given shorts at Oktoberfest to prevent upskirting
articles.summary: The step at the Munich festival comes after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.
articles.content:
The operator of a popular amusement ride at the Munich Oktoberfest has been handing out free cycling shorts to women, after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.

Some videos showing women on the Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, have been viewed millions of times. One is said to have made thousands of euros for a woman who posted it online.

The Teufelsrad is one of the oldest attractions at the Oktoberfest, the annual beer festival which comes to an end this weekend after 16 days. Its circular platform rotates faster and faster until its riders fall off, and the motion and speed often make skirts fly up.

Filming under skirts is illegal in Germany, and carries a two-year sentence in jail.

However, critics believe the law does not go far enough, and the videos of women on the Teufelsrad in their traditional dirndl dresses often show their underwear. Sometimes, the images have been digitally altered to show them naked, according to local broadcaster BR.

articles.personality_title: Munich Oktoberfest hands out free shorts to protect women from upskirting

**What happened** – To stop people from secretly filming under women's skirts, the ride operator began giving free cycling shorts to women. This new step comes after many videos showing upskirting went viral on social media, some earning money for those who posted them.

**Impact** – Giving out shorts helps protect women's privacy and dignity by making it harder to take inappropriate photos or videos. It shows how a festival can take real action to keep visitors safe, beyond just relying on laws that punish upskirting.

**What's next step** – The festival will continue this practice and may inspire other events to do the same. It could also raise more awareness about respecting people's privacy in public places.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Munich’s Oktoberfest is helping protect women from upskirting by giving free shorts, making the festival safer and more respectful for everyone.
